intro.title: A small habit. A bigger consequence.
intro.body: When we feel unwell, it can be tempting to reach for antibiotics without checking whether we need them.

habit.title: A sore throat. A busy day.
habit.body: She has some leftover antibiotics at home. Without consulting a healthcare professional, she decides to take one.

repeat.title: Then it happens again.
repeat.body: Another minor illness. Another self-directed course from the medicine drawer. Antibiotics are being used when they may not be needed.

zoom.title: A whole world, too small to see.
zoom.body: The camera follows the medicine into the body. Here, antibiotics meet bacteria — but not every bacterium is exactly alike.

exposure.title: Most are susceptible. A few are different.
exposure.body: In this bacterial population, most cells have the usual target. A small number already carry a genetic change that alters the antibiotic's target.

selection.title: The susceptible bacteria are stopped.
selection.body: The antibiotic affects bacteria it can bind to. Bacteria with the altered target are less affected and survive.

resistant.title: The survivors multiply.
resistant.body: Those resistant bacteria reproduce. Over time, they can become a much larger share of the population. The antibiotic has selected for resistance.

clinic.title: Now the antibiotic is genuinely needed.
clinic.body: She develops a bacterial infection and receives medical care. But if the bacteria causing it are resistant to that antibiotic, the medicine may no longer work.

takeaway.title: Use them only when they're needed.
takeaway.body: Never self-medicate, share antibiotics or use leftovers. Follow a qualified professional's advice. Antibiotics do not treat viral illnesses like the common cold.
